transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-14
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Menon (Nova Labs CTO), Marcus Li (Platform), Elena Ruiz (Data Scientist)
Links shared: redwood-parity-mapping.xlsx (deferred link), deck: /shared/Nova-Redwood-demo.pdf, benchmark-template.csv

Summary:
Quick migration demo to map OpenAI/Anthropic/Together API calls to Redwood endpoints; cover parity for completions, chat, embeddings, function calls, streaming, and cost/quantization options. Discussed Dedicated vs Hosted and VPC/KMS needs. Agreed to run a POC benchmark for latency/cost next week.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: All right, hey everyone thanks for joining. This is Alex from Redwood — I'll run the quick agenda: parity mapping, cost implications, console walk, and then Samir will do a short deep dive on kernels and caching.
[00:18] Dr. Priya: Thanks Alex, yes we wanted to understand how close we can get to our current OpenAI response formats and whether we lose anything moving models. Also security, we have to be SOC2 and KMS managed.
[00:29] Marcus: timeline question too — we have a pilot slated for June so we need to move fast.
[00:35] Alex: Totally. High level — Redwood exposes a single REST API that supports generation, chat, embeddings, and rerank. For migration we provide a parity mapping sheet that shows request/response fields and code snippets from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood. We'll share that after this call.
[00:50] Elena: When you say parity, do you mean identical tokens + choices arrays? We rely on the n-best choices and finish reason.
[01:02] Samir: Great question. We map the core fields — choices, usage, finish_reason — but small differences can exist due to tokenization differences across models. We include a token map and sample detokenization notes in the spreadsheet. For chat, we preserve role/name and function call payloads.
[01:20] Dr. Priya: Speaking of function calls — we use structured tool calling heavily. Does Redwood support the same semantics?
[01:26] Samir: Yes, Redwood supports function/tool calling with structured JSON. The invocation pattern is same: you provide functions schema, we return a call with name/arguments. We also stream partial call arguments if you choose streaming. Small caveat: if you rely on model-specific stop sequences, we recommend switching to structured tool calls to avoid brittle stop token behavior.
[01:46] Marcus: A lot of our traffic is embeddings for semantic search. Embedding shape and dimensionality matters — will this break the similarity index?
[01:55] Alex: We support the common embedding families. If you need identical vectors, we can pin to the same open model that you're using or provide model variants with the same tokenizer/weights. The mapping sheet lists embedding dims per model. For most customers we do a cosine similarity sanity check and recommend reindexing as part of cutover.
[02:12] Elena: Cost — how do token pricing and batching work? We're concerned about per-token cost vs latency.
[02:20] Alex: Two levers: batching and KV/prefix caching. Our Optimize recommendations give you target batch sizes to minimize GPU overhead while meeting latency SLOs. For example, a 100ms p95 target will have different batch sizing than a throughput job. We provided a simple cost model in the sheet: token price + per-request overhead.
[02:40] Dr. Priya: Can you run the example of how an OpenAI chat completions call maps to Redwood?
[02:46] Samir: Sure, quick example: OpenAI's body with messages array maps to Redwood's chat/messages param. If you have temperature/top_p they're same. The main difference is the model name mapping — we include a column that says openai:gpt-4o -> redwood/gpt4o-open weights. Also we add optional routing tags for Dedicated vs Hosted.
[03:10] Speaker 1: (mumble) question on streaming...
[03:14] Samir: Streaming is supported via server-sent events (SSE) or HTTP chunking. For function calls we can stream tokens and then a final call payload. Small transcription note: sometimes the stream ordering differs slightly, but semantics are preserved.
[03:32] Marcus: What about quantized models — we use int8 to cut costs. Any quality regressions?
[03:38] Samir: We have quantization profiles. For many llama-like families int8/awq works well; we include eval metrics per-profile. The Optimize tool will recommend a profile based on your prompt set and quality tolerances. If you need exact parity we can keep fp16, but cost will be higher.
[03:58] Elena: Any migration gotchas with Together models? I heard tokenization differs.
[04:05] Samir: Together sometimes uses a slightly different tokenizer, yes. That's in the sheet as 'tokenizer mismatch'. Our recommendation is to either pin the same model family or add a tokenizer re-run during indexing.
[04:18] Dr. Priya: Security: can we deploy in our VPC and integrate with our KMS?
[04:23] Alex: Yes — Private offering supports VPC peering and bring-your-own KMS/HSM. For auditability we ship request-level logs, redaction options, and retention controls. We'll share SOC2 artifacts and the deployment diagram after.
[04:40] Marcus: Is there a difference in SLA for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[04:44] Alex: Dedicated has SLA-backed latency and throughput and isolation. Hosted is multi-tenant with best-effort latency and burst options; we can offer reserved capacity tiers. Pricing differs accordingly — we'll include Dedicated price bands in the follow-up.
[04:59] Elena: Do you have a sample of the console for routing rules? We need rule-based fallbacks if a model fails.
[05:06] Samir: Yup — console shows a route table: by latency target, cost cap, or region. You can set automatic fallback to a cheaper quantized variant or different region. We'll demo the console in the POC run.
[05:20] Dr. Priya: About the POC — what benchmarks will you run?
[05:24] Alex: We'll run a small suite: 1) token throughput and latency p50/p95 for your representative prompts, 2) embedding throughput/recall samples, 3) quality parity tests comparing n-best outputs on your prompt set. We prefer customers provide a held-out set; otherwise we use a synthetic proxy.
[05:40] Marcus: For embedding recall, do you support exact float vectors or are vectors compressed?
[05:45] Samir: We store full float vectors for the POC, compression is opt-in. Indexing can be done with your vector DB — we provide export scripts.
[05:52] Elena: Any quirks around role/name mapping in chat when you port from Anthropic?
[05:57] Samir: Anthropic has different role semantics; we normalize roles to user/assistant/system. The mapping sheet has examples of ambiguous cases.
[06:06] Speaker 2: cough, small audio blip
[06:10] Alex: Ok wrapping up demo portion — Samir, do you want to do the kernel/caching sketch?
[06:15] Samir: Sure. At a high level, the runtime picks kernels based on architecture and sequence length. We do continuous batching and manage KV cache so multi-turn chat is fast. For models with long context we can shard KV cache across GPUs. There can be occasional off-by-one tokenization artifacts when switching implementations — we call that out in the migration notes.
[06:40] Dr. Priya: If we run on-prem, do we get the same optimizer and kernel updates?
[06:44] Samir: Private deployments get periodic runtime updates under supported releases — we decouple the control plane and runtime so we can ship patches. On-prem cadence is agreed in the contract.
[06:53] Marcus: Latency numbers — can you give an example p95 for a 2k token generation on an A100-like node?
[06:59] Samir: Roughly, depending on model family: for a 2k token pass on an unquantized LLaMA-variant you might see p95 in the 400-700ms range with batching tuned. If you quantize and use kernel optimizations that can drop materially. We'll provide sample benchmarks.
[07:20] Elena: What about request tracing — we want to correlate tokens to logs for debugging.
[07:24] Alex: Console has trace ids per request and token-level timing breakdowns, and you can export traces to your tracing backend.
[07:31] Dr. Priya: Ok, final questions — any limits on function call size or embedding batch size?
[07:36] Samir: There are practical limits tied to GPU memory. For function call payloads we recommend <= 64KB per invocation; for embeddings batch size depends on model dim — we'll provide defaults and auto-batching heuristics.
[07:50] Marcus: Who will own the POC on your side?
[07:53] Alex: I'll be the commercial owner, Samir will lead the technical POC and be the point of contact for benchmark runs. We'll also pull in a dedicated infra engineer if needed.
[08:04] Alex: Recap and next steps: I'll send the parity mapping spreadsheet + cost model, Samir will send curl examples and a benchmark plan, Nova to confirm prompts and SLA expectations. Target POC week of 5/26.
[08:18] Dr. Priya: Sounds good. Also please attach SOC2 and deployment diagram.
[08:21] Alex: Yep, will do.
[08:24] Elena: Thanks everyone.
[08:25] Marcus: Thanks.

Notes about transcription: occasional mishears (Anthorpic/Anthropic spelled odd), some overlap and short crosstalks are simplified.

End of transcript.
